newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Moscow mulls joint CIS reaction to Afghan fighting.
newsitem.headline: Moscow mulls joint CIS reaction to Afghan fighting.

text.p: Russia proposed on Tuesday that leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) meet to work out steps to prevent the upsurge of fighting in Afghanistan from spilling into former Soviet territory.

But senior Russian officials and experts appeared undecided on how Moscow should react to the fast advance of Afghanistan's Taleban guerrillas, who seized the capital Kabul on Friday, and were advancing towards the borders of CIS central Asian states.
Yeltsin, in hospital preparing for heart surgery, told Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to contact some leaders of the 12-member commonwealth, his press office said in a statement.
The Kremlin statement did not make clear when the meeting could take place or who would be invited. It did not specify who would represent Russia.
Moscow's immediate worry appeared to be about its border guards, who help patrol the uneasy frontier between CIS member Tajikistan and Afghanistan.

The border has become an effective front line in the prolonged conflict between the pro-Moscow Tajik government in Dushanbe and Afghan-based Islamic guerrillas. Dozens of Russian troops have died in rebel attacks, often backed by Afghan fighters.

Russia's national security supremo, Alexander Lebed, insisted on Tuesday that the triumph of the Taleban, a hardline Islamic group, in Afghanistan was fraught with danger for Moscow and its CIS partners in central Asia.

"If Taleban, backed by Pakistan, reaches the borders with Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, parts of which including the city of Bukhara they want to annexe, they will wipe away Russian border posts and see the road to the north free," Interfax news agency quoted Lebed as saying.

Lebed, a veteran of the Soviet Afghan war whose harsh statements on foreign policy have caused the Kremlin headaches in the past, said Russia should render all necessary help to the Afghan government driven out of Kabul last week.
Uzbekistan, which maintains contacts with Uzbeks living in northern Afghanistan and controlled by the ethnic Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum, has kept silent on the Taleban offensive.
Kazakhstan has expressed concern about developments in Afghanistan and called for a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue.
Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev and his Tajik counterpart, Imamoli Rakhmonov, discussed the situation by telephone on Tuesday, Interfax said.
Russian foreign ministry spokesman Mikhail Demurin told a news briefing that Russian government experts met on Tuesday to work out steps which could ensure the security of CIS members.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Monday that Moscow was not looking for any contacts with Taleban and would not do so in the nearest future.

But most top Moscow officials, still haunted by the memory of their ill-fated intervention in Afghanistan from 1979 to 1989, appeared extremely cautious about any suggestion of helping any of the parties in the conflict.
Demurin, in sharp contrast to Lebed's call to back the ousted Kabul government, said Russia would not get involved in the crisis in any way.
"We think that it is up to the Afghans to sort out their problems and call upon others to share this vision," he said.
